name: Sa'a
confidence_why: Ashley 2012, writing after nineteen years in the Sa'a community, places main stress on the syllable holding the penultimate mora and backs it with a table of twenty-six parsed words, whereas Ivens 1911 wrote that the accent falls on no particular syllable, a two-sentence impression a century old that Ivens 1913 repeats for neighbouring Ulawa and that no later description (Ivens 1918, Codrington 1885, Ray 1926) either confirms or contradicts.
catalog_citation: Ashley, Karen C. 2012. Semantics of Sa'a transitive suffixes and thematic consonants. MA thesis, Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics, Dallas (xviii+256 pp.). Open PDF:https://www.diu.edu/documents/theses/Ashley_Karen-thesis.pdf
catalog_locator: §2.3 'Syllable and stress patterns', pp. 22-23; Table 4 'Stress rule application', p. 24
catalog_quote: Oceanic stress is generally considered to be penultimate (Lynch et al. 2002), but many analyses ignore the numerous exceptions to such a rule. Most of these exceptions may be regularized if the penultimate stress rule is slightly modified to say that stress falls on the syllable containing the penultimate mora. If a word ends in (C)VV, it will bear the stress on the first vowel, with the other vowel sometimes sounding like a separate syllable. Either a V-V analysis or VV still puts the stress in the right place in such cases. If the final syllable only contains one vowel, the stress is on the previous syllable, but if that syllable contains a VV sequence, the stress will be realized on the first of the two vowels rather than on the vowel of the penultimate mora itself. Secondary stress is applied in trochaic feet from the left, which sometimes results in an extrametrical light syllable occurring just prior to the primary stress near the end of the word. Contiguous heavy syllables are parsed individually as full feet.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress goes to the syllable that contains the penultimate mora: with a light final syllable (CV) stress is penultimate; with a heavy final syllable (CVV, long vowel or diphthong) stress falls on that final syllable, realized on its first vowel. Where the penultimate syllable is itself VV, stress is on its first vowel. Syllables: V, CV, VV, CVV; VV = diphthong or long vowel, counted as one heavy syllable (two moras). Examples in Table 4: ka-na ('LL), tau-ri ('HL), ma-'oi L('H), ta-ka-lo L('LL), ha-'a-tau ('LL)('H), ma-raa-na L('HL).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress is applied in trochaic feet from the left, which sometimes results in an extrametrical light syllable occurring just prior to the primary stress near the end of the word. Contiguous heavy syllables are parsed individually as full feet. In very long words the foot immediately preceding an extrametrical syllable may also lose its stress in fast speech, and in extra long words the strongest secondary stress will occur initially, with successive feet generally diminishing in stress strength until the primary stress foot is reached.' (p. 23)
new_statements.exceptions: Ashley presents the moraic rule precisely to absorb the 'numerous exceptions' to a plain penultimate-syllable rule; the monosyllabic verbal particle ko is a clitic ('will attach as a clitic'); in singing, diphthong timing can differ from speech. NB contradiction with the older primary source: Ivens 1911 (Anthropos 6: 757) says 'The accent does not fall on any one syllable.. it is sufficient merely to sound every Vowel without laying special stress on any particular one', and Ivens 1913 (JPS 22: 30) repeats this for the Ulawa dialect; Ivens 1918 is silent. Ashley's is the trained-linguist, example-backed description and supersedes Ivens.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including suffixed forms, e.g. ha'aletehieu, ha'aholinge'inilana); foot parsing given for isolated words; based on fieldwork in Sa'a village, Small Malaita.
new_statements.identity_note: Ashley 2012 describes the Sa'a of Sa'a village and its neighbour A'ulupeine on the east coast of Small (South) Malaita, which she calls the purest form of the language; she treats Ulawa (ulaw1237, a Glottolog dialect of saaa1240) as a closely related variety differing mainly lexically and in vowel raising. Ivens 1911 describes the same Sa'a-village variety; Ivens 1913 (JPS 22: 30) gives the parallel 'accent does not fall on any one particular syllable' statement for Ulawa (ulaw1237).

readall_conflicts: Ray 1926 adds nothing: no stress statement for Sa'a. The pre-existing disagreement stands between Ashley 2012 (stress on the syllable containing the penultimate mora; final (C)VV stressed on its first vowel; trochaic secondary stress from the left) and Ivens 1911 (Anthropos 6: 757, 'The accent does not fall on any one syllable.. sufficient merely to sound every Vowel without laying special stress on any particular one'), with Ivens 1913 saying the same for the Ulawa dialect; Ivens 1918 and Codrington 1885 are silent. Ray's dialect remark (Pwaloto differs from Sa'a 'in accent and intonation') is consistent with either and decides nothing.
